line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 cxd4
teaches: The best answer to a gambit is often not to take it or to refuse it, but to transpose it into an opening the gambiteer did not want to play. Take the fun out of the setup rather than testing it head on.
explains: White has taken the pawn back and the gambit is over before it began — this is now a completely different opening, one where White has a broad centre and no attack. Grabbing the pawn instead is the principled test and it plays straight into the hands of someone who has studied the gambit for years. This road is far safer: less to memorise, and no way to lose in five moves to a line the opponent knows by heart.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 cxd4 d6
teaches: Against a broad pawn centre, attack the advanced pawn straight away. A centre only cramps you while it is intact, and the pawn furthest forward is always the one with the fewest defenders.
explains: Black hits the pawn on e5 at once rather than developing around it. That pawn is the one taking away squares — it denies f6 and d6 to the black pieces — and every move it survives is a move Black spends squeezed. White will have to spend time propping it up, and that is time not spent attacking.

line: e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 cxd4 d6 Nf3
teaches: When the opponent defends a pawn you attacked, you get to choose between trading it off and adding a second attacker. Trading clarifies; attacking again keeps the tension and the options.
explains: The knight comes out and props up the advanced pawn. Black now has a real choice: take on e5, which resolves the centre immediately, or bring the queen's knight out and add a second attacker instead. The knight move is the main and principled continuation, and it invites the bishop out to c4 — the position where the interesting theory really begins.
